title: GOTCHA: scraper vs raw DOM tree - index-based traversal
description:
The TS version uses raw DOM tree walking with indices (children[n]).
The Rust scraper library uses Selector + iterators, not indices.

SOLUTION: domStroll manually filters & indexes children, then accesses by position.
This works but may need tweaking if website HTML structure has unexpected text nodes.

TEST: Validate that domStroll handles text nodes correctly (should skip or error as needed).

title: GOTCHA FOUND: DOM paths off by one - all start from html but paths expect to start before it
description:
Analysis revealed the root cause of checker failures:

TypeScript domStroll:
- Receives kids = parsed document root (array with <html> element)
- path[0] = (0, 'html') means "get children[0], expect html"
- This navigates FROM before html TO html

Rust implementation:
- root_element() gives us the <html> element directly  
- path[0] = (0, 'html') tries to get html's children[0] (which is <head>)
- Result: all paths are off by one level!

Solution: Two options:
1. Remove (0, 'html') from all checker paths since we start AT html
2. Change domstroll to check first step against current before descending

Going with option 1 - simpler and clearer.
This explains all the 'not <html> (got <head>)' errors.
notes:
Root cause identified: The index values in domStroll paths are designed for html-dom-parser (TS), not scraper (Rust).

These two libraries enumerate children differently:
- html-dom-parser: May count ALL nodes including text nodes
- scraper: We manually handle both text and element nodes

Partial fix: Removed initial (0, 'html') entry since we start AT html, not before it.
Result: AHD checker now works!

Remaining issue: Other checker indices need recalibration for scraper's node enumeration.
Would require testing against live websites to discover correct paths.

This is expected when porting between parsing libraries with different APIs.

title: INVESTIGATE: Can we use smol + reqwest with default-features=false?
description:
User found that reqwest CAN work with smol if:
1. Disable default-features on reqwest 
2. Use rustls-tls instead of tokio
3. Add hickory-dns for async DNS

Current setup: tokio (heavier than needed for CLI tool)
Goal: Verify if smol actually works and is lighter

Test approach:
- Create branch with smol config
- Try the example from research
- Benchmark binary size & startup time if it works
- Decide: keep smol if benefits outweigh complexity, else keep tokio
notes:
TESTED: The research was partially correct but smol doesn't work with reqwest in practice.

Why it failed:
- reqwest 0.12 + disable default-features + rustls-tls: still pulls in tokio
- hickory-dns itself depends on tokio (via hickory-resolver, etc)
- hyper 1.x inside reqwest needs tokio for its reactor
- Fundamental issue: hyper's DNS resolver is tokio-dependent

Result: Even disabling default-features, tokio is still a transitive dependency via hyper->tokio.

Decision: KEEP TOKIO. It's fine for a CLI tool (small startup overhead, good ecosystem support).
The added complexity of forcing smol isn't worth the marginal savings.

title: DECISION: Rejected smol runtime refactor
description:
Investigated replacing tokio with smol to reduce CLI startup overhead. After testing, found insurmountable TLS dependency on tokio:

**Investigation Summary:**
- smol-hyper crate bridges executor traits but doesn't solve TLS
- reqwest + any TLS variant (rustls-tls, native-certs) → tokio-rustls → tokio (unavoidable)
- futures-rustls is runtime-agnostic but requires ditching reqwest for custom HTTP client
- Custom HTTP implementation would cost ~200+ LOC per checker (13 checkers total)

**Cost-Benefit Analysis:**
- Tokio startup overhead: ~100ms (negligible for CLI tool)
- smol doesn't matter for CLI context (not a server with 1000s concurrent connections)
- Refactoring risk: would weaken scraping reliability vs reqwest (battle-tested)
- Opportunity cost: energy better spent fixing broken scrapers (OED, Dictionary.com, Etymonline, etc)

**Decision:** Accept tokio as unavoidable transitive dependency. Do not pursue smol refactor.
Focus on fixing broken scrapers and Discord bot integration instead.

returns 403 Forbidden for all requests, including with User-Agent headers.

The TS version likely doesn't work either (or uses credentials/special access).

OED checker will return None (error) for all queries.
This is consistent with the error-handling pattern: return null on network issues.

title: Feature: Support Collins Dictionary (currently blocked by JS rendering)
description:
Collins dictionary website is entirely built with JavaScript (client-side rendering). Initial server response contains no dictionary content, only JS bundle.

TECHNICAL CHALLENGE:
- Traditional HTML scraping (via Earl + domstroll) won't work
- Would need headless browser (Puppeteer/Selenium equivalent) or API

POTENTIAL SOLUTIONS TO INVESTIGATE:
1. Use headless browser library (headless_chrome crate or similar)
2. Check if Collins has public API endpoint we can use
3. Evaluate if JS rendering approach is worth the complexity/performance cost

CONTEXT:
- Originally attempted in hippiebot.js but commented out
- Never activated due to JS rendering limitation
- See: https://github.com/hippietrail/hippiebot.js/blob/main/commands/isaword.ts#L221-L239
notes:
CRITICAL FINDING: Collins is protected by Cloudflare bot detection.

When fetching https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/ketchup:
- Initial response is Cloudflare "Just a moment..." challenge page
- Contains bot detection script requiring challenge token
- Even after solving that, content is JS-rendered (not in initial HTML)

This is a DOUBLE BARRIER:
1. Cloudflare challenge must be solved first
2. Then headless browser needed for JS rendering

Makes Collins much harder than originally thought. Not just JS rendering issue.

IMPLICATIONS:
- Standard reqwest + scraper approach won't work at all
- Would need cloudflare-scraper crate + headless browser
- Significant performance cost for any Collins check
- Effort likely not worth it compared to other improvements

title: GOTCHA: reqwest/tokio forced us to switch from smol
description:
Initial plan was to use smol (lightweight, single-threaded).
Problem: reqwest depends on tokio by default, and hyper (its HTTP layer) requires a tokio runtime.
Solution: Switched to tokio with rt-multi-thread feature.

DECISION: tokio is fine for a CLI tool. If startup time becomes issue, can revisit.
Keep code runtime-agnostic in lib.rs (only main.rs knows about tokio).

title: WordNet online deprecated - website no longer available
description:
WordNet has deprecated their online web interface (wordnetweb.princeton.edu). From https://wordnet.princeton.edu/download:

'The online version of WordNet has been deprecated and is no longer available. If you would like to use WordNet in your research, you can download the database.'

Current isaword checker queries the defunct web endpoint and returns None errors.

Options to fix:
1. Download WordNet 3.1 database and integrate as local resource (complex, adds size)
2. Remove WordNet from active checkers list (simple, loses one dict)
3. Find alternative open WordNet API/endpoint

Current impact: WordNet always returns null/error in results.
